## The NEPATEC 2.0 Dataset {footer="NEPA Phase 1 | <a href='https://huggingface.co/datasets/PNNL/NEPATEC2.0' target='_blank' style='color:#0047BB;text-decoration:underline;font-weight:600;'>NEPATEC 2.0 on Hugging Face →</a>"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**What this is:** [NEPATEC 2.0](https://huggingface.co/datasets/PNNL/NEPATEC2.0) data were created by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) and is the most comprehensive public NEPA database ever assembled.

**Why this matters:** Allows researchers to systematically analyze NEPA data at scale for the first time.

<br> 

**NEPATEC 2.0 Dataset Universe:**

- **60,000+** total federal projects 
- **140,000+** NEPA documents
- 60+ federal agencies 
- 2000–2024
- Machine-readable full text (JSON)


<br> 

**Review Process Breakdown:**

::: {tbl-colwidths="[44,19,19,18]"}
| Process | Projects | Files | Pages |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| **CE** — Categorical Exclusion | 54,668 | 73,544 | 366,876 |
| **EA** — Environmental Assessment | 3,083 | 14,242 | 469,106 |
| **EIS** — Environmental Impact Statement | 4,130 | 54,297 | 6,131,757 |
:::

::: {.caption-text}
**CE:** no significant impact anticipated · **EA:** significance uncertain, brief analysis · **EIS:** significant impacts expected, full review
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| out-width: "90%"
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(d1_figures, "00_fig_projects_by_review.png"))
```
::: {.caption-text}
All federal projects by review type
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-finding}
- **CEs account for 88% of projects but only 6% of total pages** — the vast majority of NEPA activity is routine and low-documentation by design.
- **EIS reviews are 1.3% of projects but generate 89% of all pages** — each EIS produces an average of ~1,480 pages, compared to ~152 for EAs and ~7 for CEs.
- **This dataset enables population-level analysis** of NEPA patterns for the first time — prior work relied on bespoke, often agency-specific subsets.
:::

::: {.small-text style="margin-top:0.6em; border-top: 1px solid #ccc; padding-top:0.4em;"}
Munikoti, S., Nally, D., Koneru, S.D., et al. (2025). *NEPATEC v2.0: Standardized Metadata and Text Corpus of National Environmental Policy Act Documents.* PNNL/PermitAI. [PDF](https://www.pnnl.gov/sites/default/files/media/file/PNNL_PermitAI_NEPATECv2_Public_Release_20_08_25.pdf)
:::

::: {.notes}
NEPATEC 2.0 was assembled by PNNL as part of PermitAI. The dataset converted tens of thousands of PDFs into machine-readable format with project metadata. This is the first analysis to systematically characterize NEPA review patterns across the full clean energy portfolio.
:::

## Defining Clean Energy — Tag and Exclusion System

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
**Clean Energy Tags** *(at least 1 required AND no Fossil Fuel tags)*

| Tag |
|---|
| Carbon Capture and Sequestration |
| Conventional Energy Production — Nuclear |
| Conventional Energy Production — Other |
| Electricity Transmission |
| Nuclear Technology |
| Renewable Energy Production — Biomass |
| Renewable Energy Production — Energy Storage |
| Renewable Energy Production — Geothermal |
| Renewable Energy Production — Hydrokinetic |
| Renewable Energy Production — Hydropower |
| Renewable Energy Production — Solar |
| Renewable Energy Production — Wind (Offshore) |
| Renewable Energy Production — Wind (Onshore) |
| Utilities (electricity, gas, telecommunications) |

**Fossil Energy Tags** *(any 1 excludes)*

| Tag |
|---|
| Conventional Energy — Coal |
| Conventional Energy — Land-based Oil & Gas |
| Conventional Energy — Offshore Oil and Gas |
| Conventional Energy — Rural Energy |
| Pipelines |

:::
::: {.column width="60%"}

Three additional exclusions were applied after reviewing co-occurring tag combinations:

**Exclusion 1 — Utilities + non-energy only**

- **1,623 projects** tagged *only* as Utilities AND with non-energy tags (broadband, waste management, land development) were excluded — these reflect utility-adjacent infrastructure, not energy generation.

**Exclusion 2 — Military & Defense + Nuclear**

- **481 projects** tagged as Nuclear AND Military/Defense were excluded. Most are DOE-led but involve weapons-related activities, not energy production.

**Exclusion 3 — Nuclear + Waste Management**

- ~4,000 nuclear waste projects reviewed; those sponsored by DOE's NNSA, Office of Environmental Management, and Office of Legacy Management were excluded. Only **34 projects** from this category were retained.

<br> 

::: {.callout-finding}
**Clean Energy Universe:**

- ~25,000 projects initially tagged as clean energy
- **`r n_clean_fmt`** retained after exclusion criteria
- About **10%** have only clean energy tags; the remaining 90% have at least one clean energy tag alongside other non-fossil fuel tags
::: 

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The tagging system is applied to project-level metadata and document titles/descriptions. "Clean energy" requires at least one clean energy tag AND no fossil fuel tags. Multi-tagged projects are common — a solar project on federal land might also have a "right-of-way" tag.
:::

## Lead Agencies {footer="Deliverable 1 | <a href='../reports/deliverable01.html' target='_blank' style='color:#0047BB;text-decoration:underline;font-weight:600;'>See full D1 report →</a>"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(d1_figures, "02_departments.png"))
```
::: {.caption-text}
Process type mix by lead agency
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(d1_figures, "02_department_process.png"))
```
::: {.caption-text}
Total clean energy projects by lead department
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-finding}
- **DOE accounts for 81% of all clean energy projects** — and processes 97% of those through Categorical Exclusions, likely reflecting high volumes of routine, CE-eligible actions (e.g., loan programs, grid modernization grants, Power Marketing Administrations, National Lab operations).
- **Interior handles 17%** of projects with a slightly more varied process mix: about 13% through EA and EIS reviews, consistent with its land-management mandate for large-scale renewables on federal land.
- **Most other agencies** — USDA, Army Corps, FERC — show handle reviews through primarily EA/EIS, rates well above DOE's when they serve as lead, indicating the CE-heavy pattern is specific to DOE's portfolio, not NEPA as a whole.
:::

::: {.notes}
DOE's concentration in CEs has policy implications — CE status means limited public review. The question for Phase 2 is whether this reflects genuinely low-impact projects or a systematic administrative preference.
:::

**County-level coverage:** CE 46% · EA 81% · EIS 64%. EA/EIS projects missing county data are estimated ~99% recoverable via reverse geocoding.
:::

::: {.callout-finding}
- **South Carolina leads** with 4,000+ projects — almost entirely driven by DOE's Savannah River Site nuclear facility, not renewable energy generation.
- **Western states dominate renewable-driven activity:** Washington, California, Idaho, and Colorado together account for a large share of transmission, solar, wind, and hydropower projects.
- **County-level geographic precision varies by process:** CEs frequently use legal land descriptions rather than coordinates; EA and EIS projects are far more geographically resolvable.
:::

::: {.notes}
South Carolina's dominance is an artifact of the Savannah River Site — a massive DOE nuclear facility. County coverage gaps are concentrated in CEs, where legal land descriptions are used instead of coordinates.
:::

# Deliverable 2 {background-color="#012169"}

## Programmatic & Tiered Reviews 


::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}

There are **three review types** in the NEPA review process: 

- **Standard:** Stand-alone EA or EIS covering a single project — the default NEPA approach
- **Programmatic:** Broad "umbrella" review (PEIS/PEA) covering a class of actions or a region, before site-specific work begins
- **Tiered:** Site-specific review that explicitly builds on a prior programmatic review, scoping out issues already addressed

This section examines how common these approaches are, which agencies use them, and whether they actually speed up the environmental review process.


<br> 

::: {.callout-finding}
- **Standard review is the overwhelming norm** — Almost 90% of projects use the standalone standard review process.
- For EA and EIS, **only 24%** are non-standard, just under 1/4 of reviews.  
:::


:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(d2_figures, "02_review_share.png"))
```
::: {.caption-text}
Share of non-standard reviews by lead agency
:::
```{r}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(d2_figures, "02_review_by_process.png"))
```
::: {.caption-text}
Proportional shares within EA and EIS process type
:::

:::
:::

## Are Tiered Reviews Actually Faster? {footer="Deliverable 2 | <a href='../reports/deliverable02.html' target='_blank' style='color:#0047BB;text-decoration:underline;font-weight:600;'>See full D2 report →</a>"}


::: {.callout-finding}
**Tiered EAs seem to take longer than standard EAs.** Programmatic EISs are modestly faster, but the distributions substantially overlap.

**Tiered EISs seem to take less time than standard and programmatic EISs.** Programmatic EISs are modestly faster, but the distributions substantially overlap.
:::

:::

---

## D2 Key Takeaways {background-color="#012169" footer="Deliverable 2 | <a href='../reports/deliverable02.html' target='_blank' style='color:#0047BB;text-decoration:underline;font-weight:600;'>See full D2 report →</a>"}

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Prevalence:** Only about 25% of EA/EIS projects use programmatic or tiered review — these are not the norm
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Speed:** Tiering does **not** reliably speed up review — tiered EAs take longer than standard EAs on average
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Who drives them:** Nuclear Regulatory Commission and BLM accounts for large share of non-standard reviews; mostly located in western states
:::

::: {.takeaway-box}
**Policy implication:** Expanding tiering requirements alone will not accelerate permitting without addressing root causes of EA/EIS duration
:::

# Deliverable 3 {background-color="#012169"}

## NEPA Process Types, Timelines & Generation Capacity {.full-size}

The three NEPA process types — **Categorical Exclusion (CE)**, **Environmental Assessment (EA)**, and **Environmental Impact Statement (EIS)** — differ dramatically in scope, duration, and the scale of projects they cover.

This section compares review durations, tracks how NEPA activity has changed over time (including the ARRA and IRA/BIL investment waves), and shows how generation capacity scales with review intensity.

::: {.notes}
D3 is the most data-rich deliverable — covering how CE, EA, and EIS compare on duration, how NEPA activity has changed over time, and what generation capacity is associated with each review type.
:::

---

## Process Types by Energy Classification {footer="Deliverable 3 | <a href='../reports/deliverable03.html' target='_blank' style='color:#0047BB;text-decoration:underline;font-weight:600;'>See full D3 report →</a>"}

::: {.columns}

```{r}
#| out-width: "100%"
```

::: {.caption-text}
Share of process types within each energy classification
:::

::: {.callout-finding}
- **Clean energy projects use Categorical Exclusions at higher rates** than fossil fuel or other project types, likely reflecting smaller average project footprints.
- **Fossil fuel projects show higher EA/EIS rates**, consistent with larger environmental footprints requiring more detailed review.
- CE is the dominant NEPA pathway for clean energy across all technology types.
:::

## How Long Does NEPA Review Take? {footer="Deliverable 3 | <a href='../reports/deliverable03.html' target='_blank' style='color:#0047BB;text-decoration:underline;font-weight:600;'>See full D3 report →</a>"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(d3_figures, "03_duration_summary_intervals_by_process.png"))
```
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
**Median durations:**

- CE: **~1 month**
- EA: **~14 months**
- EIS: **~34 months** (3 years) with the **90th percentile: > 7.5 years**

---

**Timeline completeness** (projects with both initiation + decision dates):

| Process | Complete |
|---|---|
| CE | 30% |
| EA | 62% |
| EIS | 48% |

::: {.caption-text}
Dates extracted via BERT NLP pipeline from document text
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-finding}
- **The CE→EA→EIS duration gradient is steep:** median durations range from ~1 month (CE) to ~14 months (EA) to ~34 months (EIS) — a 34× difference at the median.
- **The long tail drives NEPA's reputation:** 10% of EIS reviews exceed 7.5 years, but this is not typical — the median is 3 years.
- **Timeline completeness is partial:** only 30% of CEs have extractable dates; EA (62%) and EIS (48%) are better but not complete, so medians likely undercount the slowest cases.
:::

---

## NEPA Activity Over Time {footer="Deliverable 3 | <a href='../reports/deliverable03.html' target='_blank' style='color:#0047BB;text-decoration:underline;font-weight:600;'>See full D3 report →</a>"}

# Deliverable 5 {background-color="#012169"}

## Document Length & Fiscal Responsibility Act Impact {footer="Deliverable 5 | <a href='../reports/deliverable05.html' target='_blank' style='color:#0047BB;text-decoration:underline;font-weight:600;'>See full D5 report →</a>"}

The **Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 (FRA)** established the first statutory page limits for NEPA documents. This section examines whether lengths changed after FRA and how well current documents comply.

| Document | Standard Limit | Extraordinary Complexity |
|---|---|---|
| Environmental Assessment (EA) | **75 pages** | — |
| Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) | **150 pages** | **300 pages** |

**Regulatory page** *(40 C.F.R. § 1508.1(bb))*: body word count ÷ 500 — excludes appendices, tables, maps, citations

::: {.callout-finding}
This analysis uses **regulatory pages** (not raw PDF page counts) to match the statutory definition. Raw counts overstate length by 45–55% for EAs and 20–30% for EISs due to bundled appendices — using raw pages would substantially understate compliance.
:::

::: {.notes}
D5 asks: did the FRA's 2023 page limits actually change how long NEPA documents are?
:::

---

## Document Length Trends Over Time {footer="Deliverable 5 | <a href='../reports/deliverable05.html' target='_blank' style='color:#0047BB;text-decoration:underline;font-weight:600;'>See full D5 report →</a>"}

```{r}
#| out-width: "92%"
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(d5_figures, "05_pages_over_time.png"))
```

::: {.callout-finding}
**Document lengths were declining before FRA.** EA mean fell ~22% and EIS fell ~25% post-FRA, but the rolling average trend predates June 2023 — causation is uncertain.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
Small post-FRA sample: only 33 EAs and 42 EISs completed after June 2023. Conclusions will strengthen as more post-FRA documents accumulate.
:::

---

## Pre/Post FRA: Lengths & Compliance {footer="Deliverable 5 | <a href='../reports/deliverable05.html' target='_blank' style='color:#0047BB;text-decoration:underline;font-weight:600;'>See full D5 report →</a>"}

::: {.columns}


:::

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics(file.path(d5_figures, "05_fra_compliance.png"))
```

Compliance rates (post-FRA only)
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-finding}
- **EAs are largely compliant:** 76% of post-FRA EAs meet the 75-page limit — a strong signal that the rule is working for shorter reviews.
- **EIS compliance remains low:** Only 27% of EIS documents meet the 150-page limit; many fall in the 150–300 "extraordinary complexity" range, but 26% exceed even that ceiling.
- **Trend preceded the rule:** Document lengths were already declining before FRA 2023, suggesting the law may have reinforced — not initiated — shorter reviews. The post-FRA sample is still small.
:::

## Phase 1 Summary: Key Findings {.full-size}

::: {.incremental}
1. **`r n_clean_fmt` clean energy NEPA projects** documented — the portfolio is larger than previously understood
2. **DOE handles 81%**, processing 96% via CE — the story is dominated by DOE Categorical Exclusions
3. **Tiering doesn't automatically help** — programmatic/tiered reviews represent only 35% of EA/EIS and are not reliably faster
4. **Duration gradient is steep** — CE (~1 mo) → EA (~14 mo) → EIS (~3 yr median; 7.5-yr 90th pctile)
5. **Scale matches review intensity** — EIS = median 538 MW; EA = 60 MW; CE = 1.2 MW
6. **DOE is the multi-agency hub** — improving DOE-DOI-USDA coordination would have outsized impact
7. **FRA effect is real but uncertain** — document lengths fell ~20–25%; causation is not yet established; EIS compliance is low
8. **Technology matters** — transmission length predicts duration; geothermal requires multi-phase permitting
:::

## A3: Timeline Extraction Methodology

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Two-Stage BERT Pipeline**

1. **Date extraction** — identify all dates in document text with surrounding sentence context (±2 sentences)
2. **Classification** — fine-tuned BERT model assigns each date to:
   - *Initiation* — NOI, application received, scoping notice
   - *Review* — draft publication, comment period
   - *Decision* — ROD, FONSI, approval signature
   - *Other* — expiration dates, referenced past actions

**Selection rules:**

- Decision: prioritize strong signature/approval cues
- Initiation: NOI > application > scoping (in priority order)
- Fallback: use earliest review date when no initiation found
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Coverage Limitations**

::: {.callout-warning}
- **CE (30%):** Short documents have less temporal information
- **EIS (48%):** RODs often issued as separate documents not linked in dataset
- **EA (62%):** Best coverage; FONSIs typically included in the same document
:::

**Model:** BERT (bert-base-uncased), fine-tuned on manually annotated NEPA document sentences. Class imbalance for initiation dates is a known limitation.
:::
:::

## A7: FRA Regulatory vs. Raw Pages Methodology

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Regulatory Page Calculation**

1. Extract body text from OCR'd PDF
2. Detect appendix boundaries using section-header patterns (e.g., "Appendix A", "References", "List of Preparers")
3. Count words in body text (pre-appendix sections only)
4. Regulatory pages = body word count ÷ 500

**Scale of difference:**

- EAs: regulatory pages ≈ 45–55% of raw page count
- EISs: regulatory pages ≈ 70–80% of raw page count
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Known Edge Cases**

::: {.callout-warning}
- OCR errors in scanned legacy documents may produce NULL word counts
- Non-standard appendix headers may not be detected
- ~5% of cases: regulatory pages exceed raw pages (OCR text extraction artifact in table-heavy documents)
- Waivers and "extraordinary complexity" exceptions are not distinguished from standard non-compliance
:::
:::
:::

## A8: NEPA Policy Context 2025–2026 {.scrollable}

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| Jan 20, 2025 | EO 14154 revokes CEQ NEPA regulation authority; instructs agencies to eliminate permitting delays |
| Feb 25, 2025 | CEQ issues interim rule removing NEPA regulations from CFR |
| Apr 23, 2025 | DOI emergency permitting: review timelines reduced to under 1 month |
| May 29, 2025 | Supreme Court (*Seven County v. Eagle County*): agencies may limit NEPA scope to decisional authority |
| Jul 4, 2025 | Reconciliation bill signed — pay-to-play expedited reviews enacted |
| Jul 3, 2025 | DOE, DOI, USDA, Army Corps, DOT, FERC convert NEPA regulations to nonbinding guidance |
| Jul 23, 2025 | AI Action Plan: EO directs new CEs, NEPA exemption when federal funding < 50% |
| Dec 18, 2025 | SPEED Act passes House — limits on judicial review, new NEPA exemptions proposed |
| Dec 22, 2025 | DOI issues stop-work orders for 5 offshore wind projects including Vineyard Wind 1 |
| Jan 8, 2026 | CEQ adopts final rule: all NEPA regulations removed from Federal Register |

::: {.small-text}
*Source: CATF NEPA & Permitting Reform Timeline. The Phase 1 analysis predates most of these actions. Phase 2 data collection will capture their effects on permitting patterns.*
